stem: A newly developed inhaled anesthetic has an improved safety profile compared to traditional volatile inhaled anesthetics.  Preliminary pharmacodynamic properties of the agent are determined through a series of experiments on healthy volunteers.  The tests show that the agent demonstrates relatively high potency.  Which of the following parameters would best describe the potency of this agent when reporting the results of the study?​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌

options.label: E
options.text: Rate of rise in arterial partial pressure

explanation:
The potency of an inhaled anesthetic is determined by the concentration in the brain needed to achieve adequate anesthesia.  This depends largely on the drug's intrinsic affinity for CNS targets (eg, GABA, glycine, glutamate) and its overall lipid solubility.  Greater lipid solubility is generally associated with higher potency, likely because these agents interact with hydrophobic, membrane-associated regions of receptor and ion-channel proteins.

When a gas anesthetic is inhaled continuously at a constant rate over a prolonged period (ie, at steady state), its partial pressure equilibrates throughout the body (eg, alveoli, blood, brain).  Because anesthetic effect directly depends on the partial pressure in the brain (concentration = partial pressure × solubility), the alveolar partial pressure at steady state can be used to assess potency and is reflected clinically by the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC).

MAC is the steady-state alveolar concentration (ie, volume percent) of an inhaled anesthetic, measured at 1 atmosphere, that prevents movement in 50% of patients in response to surgical incision (ie, ED50).  Therefore, MAC is inversely related to potency: a less potent anesthetic requires a higher MAC, whereas a more potent anesthetic has a lower MAC.

MAC is an intrinsic property of the anesthetic that does not depend on the type of surgery; duration of anesthesia; or the sex, height, and weight of the patient. However, MAC is affected by physiologic factors, including body temperature, and generally decreases with increasing age.

(Choices A, B, and E)  The blood/gas partition coefficient corresponds to the solubility of a gas anesthetic in the blood.  Agents with a high blood/gas partition coefficient bind to plasma proteins and lipids to a greater extent, resulting in a large alveolar-arterial partial pressure gradient during anesthetic induction.  The increased time it takes for the blood to become saturated causes the partial pressure in the blood to rise more slowly, delaying the onset of action.

(Choice C)  Clearance of inhaled anesthetics occurs mainly via exhalation from the lungs into the air; hepatic metabolism of most gas anesthetics is low.  However, halothane, an older anesthetic, is metabolized extensively by the liver.

Educational objective:The minimal alveolar concentration (MAC) refers to the concentration (ie, volume percent) of an inhaled anesthetic needed to render 50% of patients unresponsive to painful stimuli.  Potency is inversely proportional to the MAC: the lower the MAC, the more potent the anesthetic.​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌
